I saw the alert this morning. My team could not create any tickets for almost three hours. What happened?
The incident was detected at 9:14, and you were notified as soon as it was confirmed. It was an integration failure after our last release.
A patch was written and tested, and it was applied at 11:40. The service was restored twelve minutes later. No data was lost.
Fine. But what stops this from happening again next month?
A post-mortem was held yesterday. A new alert was added to prevent it, and every integration change is now tested before it is released.

Hi Patrícia, this is David. I am calling about this morning. My team told me that no tickets were created between nine and twelve, and the whole support queue was frozen. I got your email at nine forty-five, so I know you were on it, and I appreciate that. But my director will ask me three questions tomorrow, and I need the answers in writing. First, what exactly happened, and when the problem was detected. Second, how it was fixed, and how long the outage lasted in minutes. And third, what was changed so that this is not repeated next month. Please keep it short and factual. If the report is clear, the conversation is closed and we move on. Talk later.

Hi Patrícia, it is Karen. I read your draft of the Northwind incident report, and it is almost there. Two things before you send it. First, give the times. A customer who is told that the service was restored at eleven fifty-two feels much calmer than a customer who is told that the team worked very hard. Numbers sound like control; adjectives sound like an excuse. Second, do not open with we made a mistake. Write what happened to the service: the sync was stopped, the tickets were not created, the service was restored. Then, at the end, one sentence about what was changed so that it does not happen again. That last sentence is the one the director reads. And remember, an apology is short. One line is enough, and then the facts. You handled this well today. Send it before lunch.
